body: The same two chords have been going round for eleven minutes now — twenty past nine on a Thursday night, a boy of seventeen still at the keys at the front of a hall where about forty people are standing. The pastor is praying with somebody down the front and has made the small circling gesture that means keep it going, so he keeps it going. He knows what the third chord does: go to it, lift the pad a little, and hands come up across the back three rows. He has known that since he was fifteen. What he is mostly thinking about is whether his lift will wait, because it is a forty-minute walk.

Nobody in that hall is being deceived and the boy is not a cynic. He loves the room and would be there anyway. But he knows which chord does it, and that knowledge has sat oddly in him for two years, and there is nobody he can raise it with.

Somewhere along the way, loudness became the evidence. If the room is not shouting, nothing is happening; if the music is not enormous, the Spirit has not come. It is an easy assumption, because the two do genuinely occur together, and many of this tradition’s best moments have been extremely noisy.

The trouble is that fire in the text is never the volume. Look at what it actually does there. It consumes an offering that had been drenched in water on purpose, before a crowd assembled to watch nothing happen. It marks a boundary at a mountain that nobody may cross. It sits on people’s heads at Pentecost without burning them, which is the whole point of the detail. In none of those cases did anybody present produce it, and in most of them they had made their best effort first and got nowhere. Fire is what arrives. It is not what a room manufactures and then measures.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations. HM 341.90 is Pentecostal Fire, assigned and in build and not yet on air, a prayer station with Morning Fire at six and a Tarry Service at nine at night in its published schedule. On the music side of the same band, HM 302.50 is Pentecostal Shout, and that one is on air today.

Which brings up the passage this tradition would rather assign to somebody else. Elijah has just had the loudest victory in the Hebrew Bible — the fire has fallen, the prophets are finished, the rain has come. Then he runs, and hides, and at the mountain the whole demonstration is staged again for an audience of one. Elijah gets wind, earthquake and fire, and the text says God was in none of them. Then a low voice, and he covers his face. That passage belongs to us as much as Acts 2 does, and owning it costs us our most reliable instrument.

Because volume is manufacturable and presence is not. Any competent musician can produce the physiological signature of a move of God in about ninety seconds — the build, the modulation, the held note, the room on its feet. It is a technique. It works on more or less anybody, and identically at a stadium concert with no theological content. Once a congregation has been trained to read intensity as presence it will need more of it next week, and the people running the room will supply it, and nobody in the building is lying. Everybody is measuring with the wrong instrument.

This band is arranged so that the shout and the still hour are not asked of the same room at the same time. They sit on different frequencies. There is a gospel station that is genuinely energetic, an ambient watch that runs through the night, and a prayer frequency in build for tarrying. A listener who wants the shout can go and get it; a listener who wants the low voice is not made to sit through a build to reach it. That is what a dial can do and a single room on a Thursday cannot.
The obvious correction is to turn everything down. It does not work either.

The quiet alternative deserves to be taken seriously, because it is not merely taste. Liturgy, silence, plainsong and the fixed hours protect people from manipulation by refusing to attempt any, and they have produced some of the deepest praying there is. Nothing here is an argument against them. But a room that never gets loud has not solved the measurement problem; it has moved the assumption to the other end and hidden it better. Hush is as manufacturable as a key change — dim the lights, drop to one sustained note, leave a long pause, and you will produce reverence in people who brought none with them. Aesthetic control is aesthetic control at either extreme.
The instrument is wrong at both ends of the dial.

It is a Sunday morning and a woman of fifty-one is at the back of a church she has been in since she was nine, with her coat still on. She is normally three rows from the front and first to answer anything said from it. Two weeks ago her son was arrested. The band is doing the thing it does. The room is up, and she can see it working on all of them, and she cannot get near it. A woman she barely knows, who does the second tea rota, comes and sits in the same row with one seat between them. She does not put a hand on her. She does not say anything at all. She stays there through the rest of it and through the notices.
There was no build in that back row. Nothing rose, nothing modulated, nobody put a hand up, and the sound desk has no record of it. Two women sat down.

The honest cost of giving up volume as the instrument is that you get nothing measurable back. You cannot run a meeting on discernment. You cannot tell the musicians on Thursday that the metric has been withdrawn and they should now play whatever is true, because that is not a playable instruction. A worship leader who stops using the tools will lead a flatter meeting, people will say so, and some of them will go where the meetings are better. That is a real cost, and pretending otherwise from a keyboard is cheap.

But the not-knowing is the instrument. You are supposed to not know. Certainty about whether God has come into a room was never on offer, and the demand for it is what makes rooms escalate: if the evidence must be visible by half past nine, somebody has to produce it. Take away the requirement to know and the pressure to manufacture goes with it. The boy at the keys can then play the third chord because the song wants it rather than because the room needs proof, which is a very different thing to be doing with two hands.

So the correction is not quieter music and it is not less of anything. This tradition has carried the gospel into more poor places, with less money, than the traditions that patronise it; it kept the supernatural on the table when respectable churches were quietly putting it away; and it raised people who actually pray. None of that is up for negotiation. What is up for negotiation is one habit of measurement — the reflex that reads decibels as arrival — and it can be dropped without losing a single thing the tradition is right about.
All of which is argument, and argument stays theory until something is actually playing.

Four kinds of programming run on this dial and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, gospel, country, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards.

So start at HM 302.50, Pentecostal Shout — and start there precisely because this article is not an argument for turning the music down. It is energetic gospel, Imani and Zariah Inspire, with Sunday Morning Gospel at eight and Gospel Fire Hour at seven in the evening. What makes it the right test is that there is no room. Nobody is leading you, nobody can see whether your hands are up, and nobody cares whether you stand. Everything the technique needs in order to work has been taken away, and what is left is whether the songs are good and whether they are true. If they still get you in a kitchen with nobody watching, it was never the technique.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it nearer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it will open like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band learns which frequencies people are really reaching for — which is how the next one gets built.

Take that as an invitation rather than a corrective. Put HM 302.50 on this week while you are cooking or driving, at whatever volume the room can take, and let it be as loud as it likes. Nobody is watching you and nothing is being built towards. Whatever happens in you while your hands are busy with something else is worth more than anything that could have been produced in eleven minutes on two chords, and that difference is the only thing this article has been trying to name.
